blocks.content: You've got 80 service instances running behind a load balancer. Something's throwing 500s for a chunk of users right now.
Where do you look? The logs. But which of the 80 machines? You don't know yet, that's the whole problem.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396349135-811197222.png
blocks.alt: Engineer trying to SSH into dozens of machines to grep logs during an incident

blocks.content: Old school move: SSH into machine 1, grep the log file, nothing. SSH into machine 2, grep again, nothing. Repeat 78 more times while the incident is still live and your users are still seeing errors.
That doesn't scale past a handful of machines. You need every log line from every instance in one searchable place, and you need it before the incident is over, not after.
Log aggregation ships logs from every instance to one centralized system where you can search, filter, and correlate across the whole fleet in a single place.
1. Introduction

Every request in a distributed system touches multiple services. A single checkout call might hit the API gateway, the cart service, the payments service, and the inventory service, each running on its own set of machines.
Each of those services writes its own logs, to its own local disk, on its own machine. When something breaks, the evidence is scattered across every one of those machines.

["The problem logs live locally on each instance, nobody can search across the fleet","The core idea ship every log line off the host to one central system","The payoff search, filter, and correlate logs across every service and every instance from one screen"]
items: The problem logs live locally on each instance, nobody can search across the fleet
The core idea ship every log line off the host to one central system
The payoff search, filter, and correlate logs across every service and every instance from one screen

blocks.title: Not just for incidents
blocks.content: Log aggregation also powers things like tracking a single request across five microservices using a request ID, spotting a slow creeping error rate before it becomes an outage, and auditing who did what.
2. The problem without a centralized system
blocks.text: 2. The problem without a centralized system

blocks.content: Picture 80 instances of the same service, all behind a load balancer, all writing to a local file like /var/log/app/service.log.
A customer reports an error. You don't know which instance handled their request, because the load balancer picked one at random. So you'd have to check all 80.

["SSH into each box one at a time","grep for the customer's request ID or timestamp","Hope the log rotated recently, or the evidence is already gone","Do this again for every downstream service that request touched"]
items: SSH into each box one at a time
grep for the customer's request ID or timestamp
Hope the log rotated recently, or the evidence is already gone
Do this again for every downstream service that request touched

blocks.title: This gets worse with autoscaling
blocks.content: If an instance scaled down and got terminated, its local disk and its logs are gone with it. You can't SSH into a machine that no longer exists.
3. The core idea: ship logs to one place
blocks.text: 3. The core idea: ship logs to one place

blocks.content: Instead of logs sitting wherever they were written, you ship them off the host as they're generated, to a central system built for search.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396349136-167036378.png
blocks.alt: A log shipping agent on a host tailing the local log file and forwarding it out

blocks.content: The app itself doesn't need to know any of this is happening. It just writes log lines to a file or stdout like it always did. A separate small agent process running on the same host does the shipping.
3.1 What changes for the on call engineer
blocks.text: 3.1 What changes for the on call engineer

blocks.content: {"headers":["Without aggregation","With aggregation"],"rows":[["SSH into every instance one by one","One search box, one query"],["Logs vanish when an instance is terminated","Logs already shipped, survive the instance"],["No way to correlate across services","Filter by request ID across the whole fleet"]]}
4. The typical pipeline
Once you accept the core idea, the pipeline shape is pretty consistent no matter which specific tools you pick.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396349136-397774041.png
blocks.alt: Full pipeline shape: host agent to buffer to index store to query UI

blocks.content: 4.1 Agent on every host

A small agent runs alongside your app on every instance. Tools like Filebeat, Fluentd, or Fluent Bit do this job. The agent tails log files as new lines get appended, or receives a log stream directly, and forwards each line onward.
4.2 A central pipeline
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396349137-441935091.png
blocks.alt: Agents on many hosts forwarding logs into one central pipeline

blocks.content: Every agent on every host points at the same central pipeline. That's the point where logs from 80 different machines start becoming one unified stream.
4.3 A buffer or queue in the middle
blocks.text: 4.3 A buffer or queue in the middle

blocks.content: Between the agents and the storage layer, there's often a durable queue, commonly Kafka. More on why that matters in the next section.
4.4 Storage and indexing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396349138-493585040.png
blocks.alt: Logs landing in a storage and indexing system, becoming searchable

blocks.content: Logs land in a system built to index and search text at scale, like Elasticsearch or Loki. This is what makes a query across a billion log lines return in under a second instead of a coffee break.
4.5 A query UI
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396349139-508939213.png
blocks.alt: An engineer querying logs through Kibana or Grafana

blocks.content: Finally, a UI like Kibana or Grafana sits on top, letting you type a query, filter by service or time range, and actually read the results.
5. Why the buffer or queue matters
blocks.text: 5. Why the buffer or queue matters

blocks.content: It's tempting to skip the queue and have agents write straight into the indexing system. Don't. Here's why.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350354-279974190.png
blocks.alt: A queue absorbing a log volume spike during an incident before it hits the indexer

blocks.content: Log volume isn't steady. It's low on a normal day and it spikes hard exactly when things are going wrong, which is exactly when an error handler starts logging a stack trace on every single request.
That's the worst possible moment for your indexing system to fall over from being hit with ten times its normal write load. A queue like Kafka sits in between and absorbs the burst.

["Durability if the indexer is temporarily down or slow, logs sit safely in the queue instead of being dropped","Backpressure handling the queue smooths a burst out into a steady stream the indexer can actually keep up with","Decoupling agents don't need to know or care how fast the indexer currently is"]
items: Durability if the indexer is temporarily down or slow, logs sit safely in the queue instead of being dropped
Backpressure handling the queue smooths a burst out into a steady stream the indexer can actually keep up with
Decoupling agents don't need to know or care how fast the indexer currently is

blocks.title: This is the same instinct as everywhere else
blocks.content: Any time you have a bursty producer and a rate limited consumer, a queue in between is the standard fix. Log aggregation is just one more place that pattern shows up.
6. Real systems people actually run
6.1 The ELK or Elastic stack
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350356-214638466.png
blocks.alt: The ELK stack pipeline: Filebeat to Logstash to Elasticsearch to Kibana

blocks.content: Filebeat ships logs off each host. Logstash optionally parses and transforms them. Elasticsearch stores and indexes them with full text search. Kibana is the UI you query and build dashboards in.

Elasticsearch indexes the full text of every log line. That's powerful, you can search for any word anywhere, but it's also expensive, because building a full text index over every log line takes real CPU and real disk.
6.2 The Grafana Loki stack
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350357-354801914.png
blocks.alt: The Loki stack pipeline: Promtail or Fluent Bit to Loki to Grafana

blocks.content: Loki takes a different bet. Instead of indexing the full text of every log line, it only indexes a small set of labels, things like service name, instance id, or environment. The actual log text is stored compressed but unindexed.

Grafana Loki markets itself as the cheaper option specifically because of this. Less indexing work means less compute and less storage, at the cost of full text search being slower since it has to scan rather than look up.
6.3 Commercial options

Datadog and Splunk offer the same shape of pipeline as a managed product. You install their agent, they handle the queue, the storage, and the UI. You pay per gigabyte ingested instead of running the infrastructure yourself.
7. Trade offs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350357-420743231.png
blocks.alt: Full text indexing versus label based indexing, cost comparison

blocks.content: Centralized log storage isn't free. At real scale, a fleet of hundreds of instances can produce terabytes of logs a day, and every one of those gigabytes costs money to ship, store, and index.

{"headers":["Approach","Trade off"],"rows":[["Full text indexing, e.g. Elasticsearch","Great for ad hoc search on any field, much more expensive to run at scale"],["Label based indexing, e.g. Loki","Cheaper to run, but you need to know your labels up front, and free text search is slower"],["Managed, e.g. Datadog or Splunk","No infra to run, but you pay per gigabyte and costs scale directly with log volume"]]}

blocks.title: A common real world response
blocks.content: Teams often log less at the source, sample high volume debug logs, or set shorter retention windows, specifically to control this cost, rather than just indexing everything forever.
8. Worked example
Say you're running 50 instances of a checkout service. Each one runs a Fluent Bit agent that tails the local log file and forwards it to Loki.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350358-644332836.png
blocks.alt: A fleet of 50 instances shipping logs through Fluent Bit into Loki, queried from Grafana

blocks.title: Incident walkthrough
blocks.text: Checkout error rate jumps at 2:14pm. You open Grafana, filter by service=checkout and level=error, and set the time range to the last 20 minutes. Instead of guessing which of the 50 instances is at fault, every instance's error logs show up in one stream, sorted by time. You spot that instance-37 started throwing a connection timeout to the payments service right at 2:14pm, and the rest is a payments service problem, not a checkout one.

blocks.content: Without aggregation, this same investigation means SSHing into up to 50 boxes to find the one that has anything useful in its logs. With it, it's one query.
9. Implementation: shipping logs to Loki
Here's a real Fluent Bit config that tails an application log file and forwards it to Loki, labeled by service name.

[INPUT]
    Name              tail
    Path              /var/log/app/checkout.log
    Tag               checkout.logs
    Refresh_Interval  5
    Mem_Buf_Limit     10MB

[OUTPUT]
    Name              loki
    Match             checkout.logs
    Host              loki.internal
    Port              3100
    Labels            service=checkout, env=production
    Line_Format       json
    Remove_Keys       tag

codes.ini:
[INPUT]
    Name              tail
    Path              /var/log/app/checkout.log
    Tag               checkout.logs
    Refresh_Interval  5
    Mem_Buf_Limit     10MB

[OUTPUT]
    Name              loki
    Match             checkout.logs
    Host              loki.internal
    Port              3100
    Labels            service=checkout, env=production
    Line_Format       json
    Remove_Keys       tag

blocks.content: The Input block tells Fluent Bit which file to tail and how often to check for new lines. The Output block points it at Loki and attaches labels, service and env, which is exactly what Loki indexes. Everything else in the log line stays as unindexed text.

blocks.title: Keep label cardinality low
blocks.content: Don't put things like request ID or user ID in Loki labels. Labels are meant to be a small, low cardinality set, like service name or region. High cardinality labels blow up Loki's index size and defeat the whole cost advantage.
10. The interview angle
In a system design interview, if you're designing anything with more than a couple of services, log aggregation is expected infrastructure, the same way a load balancer or a cache is.

["Know the shape of the pipeline: agent on host, buffer or queue, storage and index, query UI","Know why the queue is there: absorbing bursty log volume without dropping logs or overwhelming the indexer","Know the cost angle: full text indexing like Elasticsearch is powerful but pricier, label based indexing like Loki is cheaper but less flexible","Be ready to name real systems: ELK, Loki plus Grafana, or a managed option like Datadog"]
items: Know the shape of the pipeline: agent on host, buffer or queue, storage and index, query UI
Know why the queue is there: absorbing bursty log volume without dropping logs or overwhelming the indexer
Know the cost angle: full text indexing like Elasticsearch is powerful but pricier, label based indexing like Loki is cheaper but less flexible
Be ready to name real systems: ELK, Loki plus Grafana, or a managed option like Datadog

blocks.title: You don't need to design a new log system
blocks.content: The expectation isn't that you invent log aggregation from scratch. It's that you recognize it as a standard building block and can sketch its pipeline in thirty seconds when asked how you'd debug an incident across a fleet.
